BLACKLISTING A FORMER EMPLOYEE — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Taylor Morgan · Acme Corp

PURPOSE AND SCOPE OF THIS INFORMATION SHEET
This information sheet, prepared by Jordan T. Reyes, summarizes California Labor Code sections 1050 through 1054 — the statutory scheme, sometimes called the "blacklisting" statute, that makes it a crime for a former employer to prevent or attempt to prevent a former employee from obtaining new employment by misrepresentation, and that gives the affected employee a separate civil remedy. Where a specific employer and former employee are named below, those names are Acme Corp and Taylor Morgan; this sheet can also be used and read on its own, without any specific employer or employee named, as a general reference to what this statute says. This sheet states the law; it does not evaluate whether any particular communication, policy, or practice complies with it, and it is not a substitute for individualized legal advice.

CORE PROHIBITION — PREVENTING RE-EMPLOYMENT BY MISREPRESENTATION
California Labor Code section 1050 makes it a crime for any person, or an agent or officer of that person, to prevent or attempt to prevent a former employee from obtaining employment elsewhere by misrepresentation, once that employee has been discharged or has voluntarily left the job. The prohibited conduct is the misrepresentation itself, made with the purpose or effect of blocking the former employee's re-employment — the statute does not require that the attempt actually succeed; an unsuccessful attempt to prevent re-employment by misrepresentation is covered on the same terms as a successful one.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "Any person, or agent or officer thereof, who, after having discharged an employee from the service of such person or after an employee has voluntarily left such service, by any misrepresentation prevents or attempts to prevent the former employee from obtaining employment, is guilty of a misdemeanor."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 1050 (California Legislative Information text), California Labor Code (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=1050.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence that a prohibition of this kind exists in at least one jurisdiction — not a claim about which state's law governs any particular employer-employee relationship. The statute's coverage turns on the word "misrepresentation": it reaches false or misleading communications made to prevent re-employment, not merely negative-but-truthful ones, a line the companion safe-harbor provision (Labor Code section 1053, covered separately in this sheet) draws directly. Whether any given communication is a "misrepresentation" within the meaning of this statute is a fact-specific question this document does not resolve. This clause cites a single statutory section (§ 1050); the text was independently confirmed against two separately fetched copies of the official California Legislative Information page before being treated as verified.

RELATED PROHIBITION — CONDITIONING EMPLOYMENT ON PHOTOGRAPHS OR FINGERPRINTS SHARED WITH OTHER EMPLOYERS
In the same chapter as the core prohibition, Labor Code section 1051 separately makes it a crime to require, as a condition of getting or keeping a job, that an employee or applicant be photographed or fingerprinted by someone who wants that photograph, fingerprint, or related information in order to furnish it to another employer or third person — where the photograph or fingerprint could be used to the employee's or applicant's detriment. Unlike section 1050, this provision does not turn on whether a misrepresentation was made; it prohibits the underlying practice of conditioning employment on this kind of information-sharing arrangement, subject to an exception stated in a separate section of the same chapter (Labor Code section 1057) that this sheet does not independently address.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "Except as provided in Section 1057, any person or agent or officer thereof, who requires, as a condition precedent to securing or retaining employment, that an employee or applicant for employment be photographed or fingerprinted by any person who desires his or her photograph or fingerprints for the purpose of furnishing the same or information concerning the same or concerning the employee or applicant for employment to any other employer or third person, and these photographs and fingerprints could be used to the detriment of the employee or applicant for employment is guilty of a misdemeanor."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 1051 (California Legislative Information text), California Labor Code (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=1051.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence that this kind of related anti-blacklisting mechanism exists in at least one jurisdiction. The statute's own text carves out "[e]xcept as provided in Section 1057" — this sheet has not independently verified the content of section 1057 and does not describe what that exception covers; a reader relying on this section should look at section 1057 separately rather than assume no exception applies. Whether any particular photograph or fingerprint arrangement falls within this prohibition, or within the unverified section 1057 exception, is a fact-specific question this document does not resolve. This clause cites a single statutory section (§ 1051); the text was independently confirmed against two separately fetched copies of the official California Legislative Information page before being treated as verified.

LIABILITY FOR KNOWINGLY PERMITTING A VIOLATION
Labor Code section 1052 extends criminal exposure beyond the person who directly commits a violation. It is also a misdemeanor for a person to knowingly cause, suffer, or permit an agent, superintendent, manager, or employee working for that person to commit a violation of sections 1050 or 1051, or to fail to take all reasonable steps within that person's power to prevent such a violation.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "Any person who knowingly causes, suffers, or permits an agent, superintendent, manager, or employee in his employ to commit a violation of sections 1050 and 1051, or who fails to take all reasonable steps within his power to prevent such violation is guilty of a misdemeanor."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 1052 (California Legislative Information text), California Labor Code (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=1052.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of this kind of extended liability, not a claim about which state's law governs a particular workplace. By its own terms, section 1052 reaches violations of sections 1050 and 1051 only — it does not extend to section 1053, which (as the companion clause in this sheet explains) is a safe-harbor provision rather than a prohibition, so there is no "violation" of section 1053 for section 1052 to reach. What counts as "reasonable steps" to prevent a violation is a fact-specific question this document does not resolve. This clause cites a single statutory section (§ 1052); the text was independently confirmed against two separately fetched copies of the official California Legislative Information page before being treated as verified.

TRUTHFUL STATEMENT SAFE HARBOR AND ITS EVIDENTIARY TRAP
Labor Code section 1053 affirmatively permits an employer, or an agent, employee, superintendent, or manager of the employer, to furnish a truthful statement about why an employee was discharged or why an employee voluntarily left, when that statement is given upon a special request for it. The same section then creates a specific evidentiary trap: if the statement conveys information through a mark, sign, or other means different from what its words say, that fact — or the fact that information of that kind was given without having been specially requested — is prima facie evidence of a violation of sections 1050 through 1053.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "Nothing in this chapter shall prevent an employer or an agent, employee, superintendent or manager thereof from furnishing, upon special request therefor, a truthful statement concerning the reason for the discharge of an employee or why an employee voluntarily left the service of the employer. If such statement furnishes any mark, sign, or other means conveying information different from that expressed by words therein, such fact, or the fact that such statement or other means of furnishing information was given without a special request therefor is prima facie evidence of a violation of sections 1050 to 1053."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 1053 (California Legislative Information text), California Labor Code (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=1053.)
  Known gap: This clause corrects a common mislabeling: section 1053 is not itself the criminal-penalty provision for blacklisting — the misdemeanor penalty is written into section 1050. Section 1053 instead operates as a safe harbor for a specific kind of truthful, specially-requested communication, while simultaneously creating an evidentiary presumption against coded or unsolicited signals. This is one state's statute, used as real evidence that a safe harbor and evidentiary rule of this kind exists — not a claim about which state's law governs any particular reference request. Whether a specific communication was "specially requested," or used a "mark, sign, or other means" conveying information different from its words, are fact-specific questions this document does not resolve. This clause cites a single statutory section (§ 1053); the text was independently confirmed against two separately fetched copies of the official California Legislative Information page before being treated as verified.

SEPARATE CIVIL REMEDY — TREBLE DAMAGES
Beyond misdemeanor criminal exposure, Labor Code section 1054 gives the person prevented from obtaining employment a separate civil remedy: any person, or agent or officer of that person, who violates sections 1050 through 1052 is liable to the aggrieved party, in a civil action, for treble damages — three times the actual damages sustained. That civil action may be brought by the aggrieved person or that person's assigns or successors in interest, and it may be brought without first establishing any criminal liability under this chapter.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "In addition to and apart from the criminal penalty provided any person or agent or officer thereof, who violates any provision of sections 1050 to 1052, inclusive, is liable to the party aggrieved, in a civil action, for treble damages. Such civil action may be brought by such aggrieved person or his assigns, or successors in interest, without first establishing any criminal liability under this article."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 1054 (California Legislative Information text), California Labor Code (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=1054.)
  Known gap: Source-independence disclosure: this civil remedy is codified in a section of the Labor Code (§ 1054) that sits immediately after, but is textually distinct from, the misdemeanor prohibition (§ 1050) and the safe harbor (§ 1053) covered elsewhere in this sheet — it is drawn from a different statutory section, not a subdivision of one already cited. Separately, by its own text the treble-damages remedy applies to violations of sections 1050 through 1052 only — it does not reach section 1053, which (as the companion clause in this sheet explains) is a safe-harbor provision rather than a prohibition, so there is no "violation" of section 1053 to trigger this remedy. This is one state's statute, used as real evidence that a private treble-damages remedy of this kind exists in at least one jurisdiction — not a claim about which state's law governs any particular dispute, and not a calculation of what damages, if any, would be available in a specific case. This clause cites a single statutory section (§ 1054); the text was independently confirmed against two separately fetched copies of the official California Legislative Information page before being treated as verified.

CERTIFICATION
I, Jordan T. Reyes, certify that I prepared this information sheet as a summary of California Labor Code sections 1050 through 1054, for informational reference only. This information sheet does not constitute legal advice, does not evaluate the lawfulness of any specific communication or practice, and is not a substitute for consulting a person licensed to practice law in the relevant jurisdiction.

Executed on September 2, 2026 at Oakland, California.

Signature of Jordan T. Reyes: ☐ _________________________
